questions.question_text: Eleven different landmark cards are shuffled, including one bridge card. Find $P(\text{bridge})$ as a fraction in simplest form.

options.why: Reads the bridge card as an extra card on top of the eleven landmark cards, giving a total of twelve.
Counts the ten non-bridge cards, which finds the complementary event instead of the bridge card.
Treats the bridge card as a twelfth extra card and then counts the eleven cards that are not the bridge.

questions.solution_text:
There is $1$ bridge card among $11$ equally likely cards.
$P(\text{bridge})=\frac{1}{11}$

questions.question_text: Cards numbered $1$ to $14$ are shuffled. Find the probability of drawing a multiple of $4$, as a fraction in simplest form.

options.why: Counts the eleven cards that are not multiples of four, giving the complementary event.
Uses the eleven non-multiples as the total instead of all fourteen cards in the pack.
Includes 16 as a fourth multiple of four and also uses the eleven non-multiples as the total.

questions.solution_text:
The favourable cards are $4,8,12$, so there are $3$.
$P(\text{multiple of }4)=\frac{3}{14}$

questions.question_text: The six letters of PEPPER are on separate cards. Find $P(P)$ as a fraction in simplest form.

options.why: Counts P as one of three different letters instead of counting all six cards.
Counts the three P cards but leaves one card out of the total denominator.
Counts only one P card even though the word supplies three favourable P cards.

questions.solution_text:
There are $3$ P cards among $6$ cards.
$P(P)=\frac{3}{6}$
$=\frac{1}{2}$

questions.question_text: A collector's pack has $2$ bronze, $5$ silver and $3$ gold cards. One card is drawn. Find $P(\text{silver})$ as a fraction in simplest form.

options.why: Treats the three colour categories as equally likely despite their different card counts.
Uses the two bronze cards as favourable instead of the five silver cards.
Counts only one silver card rather than all five favourable silver cards.

questions.question_text: Cards are numbered from $30$ to $42$, inclusive. Find the probability of drawing a multiple of $6$, as a fraction in simplest form.

options.why: Counts only twelve cards by subtracting the endpoints without including both of them.
Omits 42 from the favourable cards even though the inclusive range contains it.
Counts the ten cards that are not multiples of six, giving the opposite event.

questions.solution_text:
There are $42-30+1=13$ cards.
The favourable cards are $30,36,42$.
$P(\text{multiple of }6)=\frac{3}{13}$

questions.question_text: Cards numbered $1$ to $16$ are shuffled. Find the probability of drawing a number that is even **and** greater than $10$, as a fraction in simplest form.

options.why: Counts every card that is even or greater than ten, taking the union of the two groups instead of their overlap.
Uses only the eight even cards as the sample space instead of all sixteen cards.
Uses only the eight even cards as the sample space and then counts the five even cards that are not greater than ten.

questions.solution_text:
The cards satisfying both conditions are $12,14,16$.
$P(\text{even and greater than }10)=\frac{3}{16}$

questions.question_text: The seven letters of JOURNAL are on separate cards. Find the probability of drawing a vowel or the letter L, as a fraction in simplest form.

options.why: Counts the three vowel cards but leaves out L from the favourable cards.
Counts only the L card and ignores the three favourable vowel cards.
Counts four favourable cards but removes one card from the total before simplifying.

questions.solution_text:
The favourable cards are O, U, A and L, so there are $4$.
$P(\text{vowel or L})=\frac{4}{7}$
